meanings.note: Refers to a place or person right next to the speaker. In spoken Korean, 여기는 often contracts to 여긴 when introducing someone. RR: yeogi.

examples.trans: Here is my office.
Please sit here for a moment.

meanings.note: A broadcasting station division that produces variety and entertainment shows, combining 예능 (variety entertainment) and 국 (department/bureau). RR: yeneungguk.

examples.trans: I work in the variety department.
There is a variety department meeting.

meanings.note: Refers to the central point of an issue or the indispensable person in a team or organization. RR: haeksim.

examples.trans: That person is the core of our team.
Please state just the key point briefly.

meanings.note: Hangul spelling of the English abbreviation PD (producer-director), the standard Korean title for a TV or radio producer. RR: pidi.

examples.trans: PD Tak Ye-jin is here.
I am a rookie PD.

meanings.note: Points to a place near the listener, and in casual or brisk speech is used to call out to someone whose name you do not know. RR: geogi.

examples.trans: Hey, you there, just a moment!
How is the atmosphere there?

meanings.note: Playful everyday word for a polka-dot pattern, used here as a quick nickname for someone wearing a polka-dot tie. RR: ttaengttaengi.

examples.trans: The polka-dot tie is cute.
Today I wore a polka-dot shirt.

meanings.note: Means to air a program or, as in 방송하는 사람, to work in the broadcasting industry. RR: bangsonghada.

examples.trans: It broadcasts every evening.
People who work in broadcasting are busy.

meanings.note: General word for a human being or people in a given role. RR: saram.

examples.trans: There are many people in the meeting room.
That person is a new employee.

meanings.note: Everyday Korean word for a mobile phone, borrowed from English 'hand phone'. RR: haendeupon.

examples.trans: Please turn off your mobile phone before the meeting.
My mobile phone keeps ringing.

meanings.note: Refers to physical vibration and, for phones, silent vibrate mode. RR: jindong.

examples.trans: Please switch your phone to vibrate.
My phone vibrated in my pocket.

meanings.note: Denotes a fundamental rule or baseline expectation. With the copula 이다, 기본이다 means 'is basic/standard'. RR: gibon.

examples.trans: Greeting others is basic in workplace life.
Being on time is standard, right?

meanings.note: Bound noun that turns a preceding modifier clause into a noun phrase. In spoken Korean, 것 is routinely shortened to 거. RR: geot; spoken geo.

examples.trans: This is mine.
It is a good thing.

meanings.note: Irregular 르-verb meaning to not know a fact, person, or rule. Here 모르나? asks a sharp, rhetorical question. RR: moreuda.

examples.trans: I did not know that fact.
Don't you know yet?

meanings.note: Colloquial television shorthand for 생방송 (live broadcast). RR: saengbang.

examples.trans: There is a live broadcast tonight.
Everyone is nervous before a live broadcast.

meanings.note: Bound noun placed after another noun to indicate an ongoing activity or time period, usually followed by 에 (중에). RR: jung.

examples.trans: I am in a meeting right now.
Please do not make phone calls during class.

meanings.note: Demonstrative pronoun referring to something near the listener or already mentioned. Routinely spoken as 그거. RR: geugeot; spoken geugeo.

examples.trans: That is my mobile phone.
That is really important.

meanings.note: Used for phones, alarms, or bells ringing. With -면 (울리면), it means 'if it rings'. RR: ullida.

examples.trans: The alarm rings every morning.
Answer right away if the phone rings.

meanings.note: Compound of 방송 (broadcast) and 사고 (accident), referring to any unintended disruption during a live show. RR: bangsongsago.

examples.trans: A major on-air accident happened during the live broadcast.
If you are not careful, it is an on-air accident.

meanings.note: Respectful, polite adjective used to apologize in workplaces and to strangers. Formal 죄송합니다 is the standard workplace apology. RR: joesonghada.

examples.trans: I am very sorry for being late.
I am sorry for the inconvenience.

meanings.note: Demonstrative determiner placed directly before a noun to refer back to something just said. RR: geureon.

examples.trans: Please do not say such things.
Did something like that happen?

meanings.note: Refers to spoken words, remarks, or a language. With 도 (말도), it means 'even that word/phrase'. RR: mal.

examples.trans: That remark is right.
I study Korean.

meanings.note: Adverb describing acting or speaking without proper thought, caution, or respect. RR: hamburo.

examples.trans: Do not touch other people's things carelessly.
You must not make promises lightly.

meanings.note: Core Korean verb meaning 'do', and with 말 (words/expressions) it means 'say' or 'use'. In 하지 말고, -지 links it to the prohibitive auxiliary 말다. RR: hada.

examples.trans: I work.
What are you doing now?

meanings.note: Auxiliary verb used after -지 to tell someone not to do something. Ending with -고 (말고) gives a brisk, trailing command. RR: malda.

examples.trans: Please do not worry.
Do not be late, and come early.

meanings.note: Natural exclamation used when suddenly remembering, realizing, or reacting to something. RR: a.

examples.trans: Oh, now I remember.
Oh, really?

meanings.note: Humble first-person pronoun used when speaking politely to colleagues, seniors, or strangers. RR: jeo.

examples.trans: I am a new employee.
I will get in touch.

meanings.note: Compound of 차 (car) and 주 (owner), commonly used in parking and traffic situations. RR: chaju.

examples.trans: I called the car owner.
The car owner has not arrived yet.

meanings.note: Covers reaching out by phone call, text message, or chat app. RR: yeollakhada.

examples.trans: I contacted them again later.
Please contact me when you arrive.

meanings.note: Spontaneous exclamation of mild surprise or puzzlement when noticing something unexpected. RR: eo.

examples.trans: Huh? Where is my phone?
Oh? It is raining.

meanings.note: Introduces a contrast, unexpected turn, or new topic. In everyday speech it is very often contracted to 근데. RR: geureonde; spoken geunde.

examples.trans: I contacted them. But there is no reply.
By the way, what time is it now?

meanings.note: Short-form negation adverb placed directly before a verb, adjective, or status noun like 읽음. RR: an.

examples.trans: I have not read the message yet.
It is not raining today.

meanings.note: Nominalized form of 읽다 (to read), used on Korean messaging apps to show a message has been read. 안 읽음 means 'unread'. RR: ilgeum.

examples.trans: The message is still unread.
It just changed to read.

meanings.note: Adverb used in standard polite Korean farewells: 안녕히 가세요 (to someone leaving) and 안녕히 계세요 (to someone staying). RR: annyeonghi.

examples.trans: Goodbye! (to someone leaving)
Good night. (Sleep well.)

meanings.note: Basic verb of motion. With the respectful ending -세요 in 안녕히 가세요, it forms the polite farewell 'Goodbye!'. RR: gada.

examples.trans: I am going home.
Go safely!
